To: Shared/Ops & HR
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: DRAFT for Brian — Monday at Embakasi: casuals’ pay and Kisumu loading

Brian,

Thanks for taking this on while I’m away. I know you’ll be there from 5:30, and I’m sorry to leave you with a difficult morning. Please read this on Sunday. It’s a draft for now; I’ll go through it tonight before we use it.

The main thing is to go in straight and without getting defensive. This is our mess, not theirs. The guys did nothing wrong. Some are facing rent and other bills, and they have heard promises before that weren’t kept. Let them speak, apologise properly, and tell them only what we know.

What happened and what we know

Friday’s bank file for 212 casuals was rejected at validation because the beneficiary reference field was too long for the bank’s new template. None of the payments in that file was processed. Finance saw the rejection after the bank’s cut-off, so the Friday payment could not be completed that way.

Management has approved payment through M-Pesa instead. Kevin’s realistic expectation is that the money will be on phones by 11am Monday. That is not a guarantee that every person will receive it by then: the numbers must be right, and we still need to check with Finance on the batch and deal with any failed payments. Please get an update from Kevin on Monday and tell the group promptly if the position changes.

The approved batch also includes KES 500 per person for Monday lunch and fare for every casual on the affected list. The company is paying the M-Pesa charges; they must not be deducted from anyone’s pay.

Peninah has confirmed 198 numbers. She could not reach the other 14, mostly new loaders from Athi River. She’ll be at Embakasi from 7:30 with the list, so those people can give her their correct numbers face to face. Please make sure they know where to find her, without reading their numbers out to the group. She’ll also have her laptop for anyone who wants a printed payslip. Confirm with Peninah and Kevin how the 14 will be included or followed up once their details are corrected; don’t assume their payments will land with the rest.

What you can say

Please give the management apology in person. Use your own words, but something like:

“Friday’s payment did not go through. The bank rejected our payment file, and we did not catch it in time to fix it before the cut-off. I’m sorry. This is our mistake, and I understand that being without your money has put you in a difficult position.

“We’ve approved payment by M-Pesa. Finance expects the money to reach phones by 11am today, but I won’t promise an earlier time or tell you every payment is complete until we’ve checked. Everyone on the affected list is also to receive KES 500 for Monday’s lunch and fare, in the payment batch. The company will pay the M-Pesa charges.

“Peninah will be here from 7:30 with the list. If we haven’t confirmed your number, please see her privately so we can correct it. If you want a printed payslip, ask her as well. I’ll update you as soon as I have a confirmed update from Finance, even if the news is that we are still waiting.”

Then listen. Don’t argue with anyone about whether they should be angry, and don’t ask them to take our word for it without acknowledging what happened.

What not to promise

Don’t promise “by lunch,” before 9, or any other earlier time. We remember Mombasa in 2024: the supervisor said “by lunch,” the money came at 4pm, and half the shift sat down. We cannot repeat that.

Don’t say the money has been sent, that everyone will receive it by 11, or that an individual payment has succeeded unless Kevin or Peninah has confirmed it. Don’t invent an explanation for a delay or promise a remedy we haven’t approved. If you don’t know, say so, find out, and come back to them. And no threats about contracts or dismissal on Monday.

Monday morning and the Kisumu trucks

Please speak to Ouma privately first, before addressing the whole group. He’s loud, but he’s not a bad man. He has four kids and rent to think about. Hear him out, give him the same honest position on the pay, and ask what he and the others need to know. Don’t present the private conversation as a deal or ask him to make promises on everyone else’s behalf.

Joseph has been hearing the concerns already; bring him in so you know what is happening on the ground. Then address the group, apologise and explain the position. Make sure people know Peninah arrives at 7:30, especially the 14 whose numbers haven’t been confirmed. Agree a clear time and place for your next update and keep it, even if you have no new answer yet.

The Kisumu trucks are due to leave at 9am to make the mill’s offloading slot, which is before the expected payment time. Don’t imply that the trucks can wait until everyone has been paid without consequences, and don’t promise the guys payment before loading. Ask whether they are willing to load while the payment is being followed up, but don’t turn that into an ultimatum.

If Ouma’s group refuses to load, keep things calm and safe. Do not threaten anyone’s contract or dismiss anyone. Under our procedure, a stoppage is handled by Operations and HR together; it is not the grievance channel. Bring HR in immediately and handle it jointly rather than trying to settle it as an Operations-only disciplinary matter. Ask Joseph to help establish who is affected and what is needed, and keep the group informed about who is dealing with the stoppage and when you’ll return with an update. Individual pay grievances can go to Joseph as shift supervisor and then to HR within 48 hours.

At the same time, assess with Operations what the refusal means for the 9am departure and the mill slot. Escalate the risk early so the relevant people can make arrangements; don’t wait until 9 to say the trucks may be late. Be factual with both the team and the affected operation about what is known and what remains uncertain.

If anything changes, WhatsApp me before I board. I’m up from 4:30; my flight is at 7:05, so please reach me as early as you can. After that, keep HR and Finance closely involved on site and make sure there is an owner for the next update and for every unresolved payment.

Thank you, Brian. I know this won’t be an easy conversation, but a straight apology and the truth are the place to start.

Achieng
